body:
Observing Water Resources

Water resources change with rainfall, seasons, irrigation and human use. Repeated satellite images help identify the visible extent of reservoirs, lakes, rivers and other surface-water bodies. Comparing observations from different dates can reveal expansion, contraction or changes in surrounding land use.

Gujarat includes major river systems such as the Narmada, Tapi and Sabarmati, along with large irrigation networks and numerous local water-storage structures. Satellite observations can support the monitoring of reservoir surroundings, surface-water availability and land affected by irrigation.

In a dry region, a district administration may need to identify watersheds where soil and water conservation measures would be useful. Satellite images can help map drainage patterns, vegetation and land cover. These layers can be combined with rainfall records, terrain information and field surveys to support planning.

Groundwater: What a Satellite Can and Cannot Measure

Satellite-based maps can provide indirect indications relevant to groundwater prospects. Geological features, surface drainage, landforms and vegetation conditions may help identify areas worthy of investigation. However, an ordinary optical satellite image does not directly show how much usable groundwater is present in an individual borewell.

Groundwater assessment also requires geological knowledge, appropriate surveys, well observations and other local evidence. A map of groundwater-prospect zones expresses an assessment of possibilities, not a guarantee of water at every mapped location.

Land Cover and Land Use

Land cover describes the physical material visible on the Earth's surface, such as vegetation, bare ground, water or buildings. Land use describes how people use land, such as for agriculture, housing, industry or transportation.

A satellite can often identify a built-up surface, but the image alone may not prove whether a building is residential, commercial or institutional. Land-use classification may therefore require additional records or local knowledge.

There is also an important distinction between recorded forest area and actual forest cover. Recorded forest area is land recorded as forest in government records, whereas forest cover comprises land of at least 1 hectare with tree canopy density of at least 10%, irrespective of ownership or legal status. A change in administrative classification does not necessarily mean an equal change in actual tree cover.

Similarly, official land-use records distinguish net area sown, current fallow, other fallow land and land used for non-agricultural purposes. Satellite imagery may help monitor cultivation, but the correct official category must be interpreted according to its definition.

Monitoring Urban Expansion

Urban development changes agricultural fields and open spaces into roads, housing, industrial areas and public facilities. Satellite images taken at different dates can show the spatial pattern of expansion.

For Gujarat's cities, including Ahmedabad, Surat, Vadodara and Rajkot, this type of analysis can help planners understand where built-up areas are spreading and how development relates to roads, drainage and remaining open land.

A useful urban-planning GIS can combine satellite-derived built-up areas with information on transport, water supply, drainage, schools, hospitals and administrative boundaries. The resulting maps help identify infrastructure needs and possible land-use conflicts.

NUIS, AMRUT and Bhuvan

The National Urban Information System (NUIS) was initiated in 2006 by the Ministry of Urban Development to create urban geospatial databases. Its programme included 1:10,000-scale mapping for 152 towns. The Bhuvan-NUIS application made relevant geospatial information available for urban planning and master-plan preparation.

AMRUT stands for Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation. Launched in 2015, it focused on urban basic services and improvements. GIS-based master-plan preparation became an important application of geospatial technology associated with the mission.

Bhuvan, developed by NRSC, provides access to thematic and spatial datasets. It should be understood as a geospatial information platform, not as a separate satellite or launch vehicle.

BISAG-N's Role in Geographic Planning

BISAG-N, Gandhinagar, develops geospatial databases that can include village maps, survey-related information, terrain characteristics, agriculture, water resources, infrastructure and urban facilities. It also supports systems for geographic planning and monitoring.

In practice, a planning exercise may combine satellite imagery with official departmental data. For example, the location of existing water structures can be compared with drainage patterns and village requirements. The satellite data assists the analysis, while the responsible authorities verify records and implement approved works.

Prelims focus

  • Land cover describes the physical surface; land use describes its purpose.
  • Recorded forest area and actual forest cover are not identical.
  • Satellite images directly observe surface features but do not automatically establish groundwater availability.
  • NUIS began in 2006 and included 1:10,000-scale mapping for 152 towns.
  • AMRUT was launched in 2015; GIS supports urban planning under the mission.
  • Trap: A thematic map or satellite image does not replace verified land records.

[NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, chapter 5, Land Resources and Agriculture, pp. 40-44, and chapter 6, Water Resources; NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, chapter 4, Maps, pp. 24-27; NRSC, Urban and Infrastructure Applications, NUIS and AMRUT Cities sections; NRSC, Bhuvan Store, Urban Data Products; BISAG-N, Functional Unit, Centre for Geo-informatics Applications; consulted 4 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Visible land cover and officially recorded land use need not describe the same property.

pictures.alt: Five geographic layers combine with official records in GIS to identify planning needs and conflicts, with NUIS and AMRUT milestones below.

title: Satellite Mapping of Water, Land Use and Urban Development in Gujarat

body:
Why Gujarat's Coast Requires Geospatial Monitoring

Gujarat has an extensive coastline along the Arabian Sea, including the Gulf of Kachchh and the Gulf of Khambhat. Its coastal environments include ports, fishing settlements, tidal flats, creeks, mangroves, beaches and industrial areas.

Coastal conditions change because of tides, waves, sediment movement, storms and human activity. Satellite observations can help monitor these changes over large areas and compare conditions between different dates.

Important applications include shoreline monitoring, mapping of mangroves and coastal wetlands, identification of changes in coastal land use, study of sediment movement and assessment of areas affected by coastal flooding.

Shoreline Change and Mangroves

Shoreline erosion occurs where coastal material is removed faster than it is deposited. Accretion occurs where material accumulates and the shoreline advances. Both processes may be influenced by waves, currents, river sediment supply and coastal structures.

Repeated satellite images can identify broad patterns of erosion and accretion. However, the apparent waterline changes with the tide. Reliable comparison therefore requires attention to image dates, tide conditions and the definition of the shoreline being mapped.

Mangroves are salt-tolerant coastal plants found in suitable intertidal environments. They provide habitat for marine organisms, help stabilise sediments and can reduce some impacts of waves and coastal erosion. Remote sensing can help map their extent and monitor changes in cover.

Coastal wetlands and mangrove areas should not be classified solely from one colour in an image. Seasonal conditions, water levels and field observations are important for accurate interpretation.

Oceansat and EOS-06

EOS-06, also called Oceansat-3, was launched on 26 November 2022. It carries instruments for ocean observations, including an Ocean Colour Monitor and a scatterometer.

Ocean-colour observations can help estimate the concentration of chlorophyll-a, which is associated with phytoplankton. Phytoplankton are microscopic organisms that form an important foundation of marine food chains. The scatterometer measures information about ocean-surface winds.

These observations are useful for studying marine productivity, ocean conditions and developing weather systems. Chlorophyll concentration is an environmental indicator; it is not itself a direct measurement of the number of fish present.

Potential Fishing Zone Advisories

Potential Fishing Zone (PFZ) advisories identify marine areas where environmental conditions may be favourable for fish aggregation. They use information including sea-surface temperature and chlorophyll, together with oceanographic analysis.

In India, PFZ advisory services are provided by the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), an autonomous institution under the Ministry of Earth Sciences. INCOIS is not an ISRO centre, although satellite observations are important inputs to its services.

For fishermen operating from the Gujarat coast, such advisories can help identify potentially productive fishing areas. They do not guarantee a catch, and decisions at sea must also consider weather warnings, safety, fishing restrictions and local conditions.

Satellite Navigation at Sea

NavIC provides positioning and timing information that can support marine navigation. Its role differs from that of PFZ advisories. A navigation receiver helps determine where a vessel is; an oceanographic advisory identifies where fishing conditions may be favourable.

Satellite observations can also help monitor the development of coastal hazards. Weather satellites support cyclone monitoring, while radar observations help identify inundated areas after storms. These applications are examined further in the study of disaster response.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarat's coastline includes the Gulf of Kachchh and Gulf of Khambhat.
  • Remote sensing supports shoreline, mangrove and coastal-wetland monitoring.
  • EOS-06 or Oceansat-3 was launched on 26 November 2022.
  • Ocean-colour measurements help estimate chlorophyll; scatterometer data provide ocean-surface wind information.
  • INCOIS, under the Ministry of Earth Sciences, issues Potential Fishing Zone advisories.
  • Trap: PFZ identifies favourable conditions, not a guaranteed fish catch; NavIC provides navigation rather than fish detection.

[ISRO, Monthly Dynamics of the Global Biosphere on Land and Oceans using Oceansat-3, 12 March 2024; ISRO, EOS-06 images Cyclone Mandous and detects Algal Bloom, 8 December 2022; ISRO, Launch Missions, PSLV-C54/EOS-06 entry; INCOIS, Potential Fishing Zone Advisory WebGIS and PFZ information; BISAG-N, About Us, resource and environment management applications; consulted 4 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Gujarat's coastal landscapes support fisheries, settlements, wetlands and mangrove ecosystems.

title: Gujarat's Coast, Marine Resources and Satellite-Based Ocean Applications

body:
How Space Technology Supports Disaster Management

Disasters may affect large regions, damage infrastructure and interrupt communication. Satellite systems provide a broad view of changing conditions and help authorities obtain information when ground access is difficult.

Space-based disaster support generally has several functions: monitoring hazards before or during an event, mapping affected areas, locating exposed settlements and infrastructure, and comparing conditions before and after damage.

The relevant satellite depends on the problem. Meteorological satellites observe clouds and atmospheric conditions. Earth-observation satellites map land and water. Navigation satellites help with positioning. Communication satellites can support information exchange when suitable services remain available.

Cyclone Monitoring and Warnings

Over the Arabian Sea, weather-satellite observations help meteorologists study cloud organisation, atmospheric conditions and the development of storms. Geostationary meteorological satellites are particularly valuable because they can observe the same broad region repeatedly.

INSAT-3DS is an example of an Indian meteorological satellite supplying relevant observations. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) is responsible for official meteorological forecasting and cyclone warnings in India. ISRO provides satellite systems and data; it should not be confused with the authority issuing every public weather warning.

For Gujarat, cyclone-related mapping is important because coastal settlements, ports, roads, agricultural areas and electricity infrastructure may be exposed to strong winds and flooding. The risk at a particular location depends on the storm and local conditions.

Flood Mapping During Cloud Cover

Floods often occur during heavy rainfall, when thick clouds obstruct optical satellite images. Radar satellites can obtain measurements through most cloud cover and are therefore especially useful for identifying inundated land.

Flood-inundation maps show areas covered by water at the time or period represented by the observations. Comparing images from successive dates can help estimate the spread or recession of flooding.

These maps can be combined in a GIS with roads, villages, schools, hospitals and other facilities. The resulting information can support decisions about access routes, relief priorities and damage assessment.

Other Important Disaster Applications

HazardUseful space-based informationImportant limitation
Agricultural droughtVegetation condition, rainfall patterns and soil-moisture indicatorsCrop stress requires seasonal and local interpretation
Forest fireThermal observations and active-fire locationsFire detections require interpretation and appropriate response
LandslideTerrain, land cover, slope-related information and event mappingA susceptibility map does not predict the exact time of failure
EarthquakeSurface deformation and post-event damage observationsSatellites do not reliably predict an earthquake's exact occurrence
CycloneCloud patterns, atmospheric observations and coastal inundationSatellite imagery is one input to official forecasts and warnings

NRSC, NDEM and Gujarat's Disaster Institutions

NRSC operates a Disaster Management Support programme involving satellite-based information for floods, cyclones, droughts, forest fires, landslides and other hazards.

The National Database for Emergency Management (NDEM) is a national geospatial information system developed to support disaster and emergency management. It brings together geographic databases, satellite-derived information and decision-support tools. NRSC works with relevant government agencies, including the Ministry of Home Affairs, in this system.

In Gujarat, the Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority (GSDMA) and other responsible state and district authorities undertake disaster-management functions. They may use information supplied through national space-based systems and geospatial institutions.

BISAG-N supports disaster-management applications by preparing and combining geographical information for assessment and planning. It may help relate hazard maps to settlements, infrastructure and administrative boundaries.

An example is Cyclone Biparjoy in 2023. NRSC published satellite-based views of flood inundation in Gujarat associated with the cyclone. Such maps help describe an event's effects; they are not the same as a prediction that a particular structure will be damaged.

Applying the Correct Institution to the Correct Task

A useful way to understand the whole subject is to follow the movement of information from space to the public service it supports.

  • Satellite and instrument development: ISRO centres, including URSC and SAC.
  • Launch: SDSC-SHAR and the appropriate Indian launch vehicle.
  • Earth-observation data processing: NRSC and related ground systems.
  • Geospatial analysis: NRSC, BISAG-N and other authorised users of geographic information.
  • Sector-specific service: MNCFC for agricultural forecasting, INCOIS for marine advisories and IMD for weather forecasts and warnings.
  • Local public action: Relevant state departments, district authorities and other responsible agencies.

The same satellite observations may support several applications. For example, a radar image of coastal Gujarat could be relevant to flood assessment, agricultural damage evaluation and wetland monitoring. The measurement is shared, but each application asks a different question and may require different supporting data.

Integrated Distinctions for Objective Questions

Launch versus operation: A satellite may be launched successfully without reaching its final operational orbit.

Observation versus navigation: Earth-observation satellites measure surface or atmospheric conditions; navigation satellites transmit signals used to determine position and time.

Space agency versus user agency: ISRO develops space systems, while agencies such as IMD, INCOIS and government departments use relevant information to provide particular services.

Data versus decision: A satellite image supplies observations. A classification, forecast, official land record or administrative decision requires further interpretation and, where appropriate, verification.

Prelims focus

  • IMD issues official meteorological forecasts and cyclone warnings; ISRO supplies space-based observations.
  • Radar satellites are valuable for flood mapping during cloud cover.
  • NDEM is a national geospatial system supporting emergency management.
  • NRSC provides space-based disaster information; BISAG-N supports geospatial analysis.
  • GSDMA is a Gujarat disaster-management institution.
  • Trap: Satellite-based earthquake damage assessment is not the same as reliable prediction of an earthquake's exact time.

[NCERT, Science, Class 7, chapter 8, Winds, Storms and Cyclones, pp. 81-86, 2018-19 reprint; NRSC, Disaster Management Support, Applications, NDEM, Floods, Cyclones, Agricultural Drought, Landslides and Earthquakes sections; NRSC, Disaster Management Support, Gujarat flood inundation during Cyclone Biparjoy, 2023; BISAG-N, About Us, Disaster Management section; ISRO, Spacecraft Missions, INSAT-3DS and NISAR entries; consulted 4 November 2026.]
